title: Why Does the Axolotl Never Grow Up? 🦎
description:
Why does the axolotl never grow up? This smiling salamander keeps its baby gills its whole life, because its body barely sends the thyroid hormone signal to grow up.

Follow Zorbly for a new mystery every day.

tags: why does the axolotl never grow up
pinned_comment: Be honest: would you stay a kid forever, or grow up?
topic: Why does the axolotl never grow up? (neoteny: low thyroid hormone signal, keeps larval gills for life, still breeds; 1865 Paris metamorphosis)
script:
You grew up. This axolotl refuses to, for 15 years.
Most salamanders hatch in water,
then lose their gills and crawl onto land.
But the axolotl keeps its feathery gills,
its tail fin, and its baby face,
its whole life.
The reason is a tiny switch.
Growing up needs thyroid hormone,
and an axolotl's body barely sends that signal.
So it just skips adulthood,
and still has babies of its own.
In 1865, scientists in Paris got a shock.
A few of their axolotls suddenly lost their gills,
and walked out as land salamanders.
So the switch was never broken.
Would you rather stay a kid forever, or grow up?
key_facts: Axolotls are neotenic/paedomorphic: they keep larval traits such as external gills and a tail fin, and never naturally metamorphose, yet become sexually mature (~1 year) (NHM London)
Axolotl paedomorphosis is linked to low thyroid hormone signalling; metamorphosis can be induced with thyroid hormone or iodine (Frontiers in Endocrinology 2019, 'Forever young')
In 1865, some axolotls kept by Auguste Duméril in Paris metamorphosed into land-dwelling salamanders, surprising scientists (Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology 2022 review)
Wild axolotls live only in the canals of Xochimilco, Mexico City, and are Critically Endangered
